cards.q: Prevalence 1%, sensitivity 99%, false positive rate 5%. What is P(disease | positive)? Use 10,000 people.
cards.a: Sick: 100, of whom 99 test positive. Healthy: 9,900, of whom 495 test positive. P = 99 / (99 + 495) = 16.7%. Sensitivity alone hides the base rate, so always ask for prevalence and precision.

cards.q: When do you use permutations and when combinations? Count choosing 2 of 3 items both ways.
cards.a: Permutations when swapping the chosen items changes the outcome (first and second prize): 3 × 2 = 6. Combinations when it does not (a committee): 3. Test with a tiny case and list it by hand.

cards.q: When is a Poisson model a poor choice for counts, and how do you check quickly?
cards.a: Poisson has mean = variance. If the sample variance is far above the mean (clumpy counts, bursts), Poisson under-estimates risk. Compare the sample mean and variance first; consider the negative binomial.

cards.q: Revenue per order is positive and right-skewed. How do you check whether a log-normal fits better than a normal?
cards.a: Plot a histogram of the log of the data. If it looks bell-shaped, the data is log-normal. Then summarize with the median or geometric mean, not mean ± 2 SD of the raw values.

cards.q: What is the difference between SD and SE of the mean? If SD = 100 and n = 400, what is SE?
cards.a: SD describes the spread of individual values. SE = SD / √n describes how much the sample mean varies: 100 / √400 = 5. Mixing them up misreports uncertainty by a factor of √n.

cards.q: Why is a million-row biased sample worse than 200 random rows?
cards.a: Bias does not shrink as n grows. A huge biased sample gives a precise but wrong answer and false confidence. Check how the data was collected before checking how much of it you have.

cards.q: Which t-test do you use for two independent groups with possibly unequal variances? Should an F-test decide?
cards.a: Welch's t-test, which does not assume equal variances. Using the F-test for equal variances as a gate before a t-test is fragile. Just use Welch.

cards.q: Compare chi-square tests of 55 heads in 100 flips and 550 in 1,000 against a fair coin. What do you learn?
cards.a: χ² = 1.0 (p ≈ 0.32) for n = 100, but χ² = 10.0 (p ≈ 0.0016) for n = 1,000. Same 55%, very different evidence. That is why the test needs raw counts, not percentages.

cards.q: When do you use a paired t-test, and what do you lose by using an unpaired test on paired data?
cards.a: Use it when each observation in one group is linked to one in the other (same user before and after). An unpaired test throws away that link, keeps between-subject noise and loses power.

cards.q: Why report an effect size and interval rather than only 'p < 0.05'?
cards.a: p tells you only that an effect is detectable, not whether it matters. With huge samples a trivial difference gives a tiny p. Report the size (minutes saved, Cohen's d) with its interval.

cards.q: What does Benjamini-Hochberg control, and when do you prefer it to Bonferroni?
cards.a: BH controls the false discovery rate: the expected share of false positives among your discoveries. Bonferroni controls the chance of any false positive and becomes very strict with thousands of tests. Prefer BH for shortlists.

cards.q: A model has R² = 0.9. Why can't you call it a good model yet?
cards.a: R² can be high because of a shared trend or overfitting, and a low R² can still hold a useful slope. It says nothing about the assumptions or causality. Check residual plots and held-out error.

cards.q: In OLS, do you test normality on y or on the residuals? Which assumptions matter most?
cards.a: On the residuals, not raw y. Normality of errors matters least. Linearity and equal variance matter more, and independence matters most for correct p-values.

cards.q: What does a coefficient of 0.15 minutes per order mean? Why can't you compare it directly with a dummy's 40?
cards.a: It is the change in y per one-unit rise in that predictor, holding the others fixed. Raw coefficients on different scales are not comparable. Standardize predictors or compare effects over realistic ranges.

cards.q: Why standardize features before ridge or lasso, and with which statistics?
cards.a: The penalty treats all coefficients alike, so units matter: floor area (30 to 300) and rooms (1 to 8) get penalized unequally. Standardize with training-set mean and SD only, then reuse the same numbers on test data.

cards.q: Lasso keeps one of two highly correlated features. Is it the true cause?
cards.a: No. Among correlated features lasso picks one more or less at random, and the dropped one may be just as useful. Selection serves prediction, not causal proof. Elastic net spreads weight across correlated features.

cards.q: A logistic model moves p from 0.342 to 0.467, an odds ratio of about 1.7. Is the probability 1.7 times higher?
cards.a: No. The probability rises about 1.4 times (0.467 / 0.342). Odds are not probabilities; they are close only when events are rare. Read exp(coefficient) as an odds ratio.

cards.q: What is perfect separation in logistic regression, and what do you do about it?
cards.a: One feature splits yes from no without error, so the maximum-likelihood estimate does not exist: the coefficient heads to infinity and software warns or reports huge numbers. Add a penalty or rethink the feature.

cards.q: A Beta(2, 8) prior meets 30 successes in 100 trials. What is the posterior and its mean?
cards.a: Beta(2 + 30, 8 + 70) = Beta(32, 78), with mean 32 / 110 = 0.29, between the prior mean 0.20 and the data rate 0.30. Read a + b as the prior's pseudo-sample size.

cards.q: Is a Bayesian A/B test immune to peeking? What should you fix in advance?
cards.a: No. Early on P(B > A) wanders, so stopping the first time it reaches 95% is still biased. Bayesian methods suffer less than p-values, but fix a minimum sample or an expected-loss threshold before you start.

cards.q: Why is a random train/test split wrong for a time series? What do you do instead?
cards.a: It lets the model see the future and neighbouring points, so scores look better than reality. Split by time: train on the past and test on later months, or use rolling-origin cross-validation.

cards.q: What happens if you difference a series that is already stationary?
cards.a: You add noise and create a strong negative autocorrelation at lag 1. Use d = 1 or 2 only when the plot and tests demand it.

cards.q: In an ACF plot with 20 lags, one bar crosses the 95% band at lag 13. Is that a pattern?
cards.a: Probably not: about 1 bar in 20 crosses by chance. A lone bar at an odd lag is not a pattern. Look for repeated, structured spikes, and make the series stationary first.

cards.q: Why is 'average tenure of customers who already left' a biased estimate?
cards.a: It ignores customers who are still active, whose full tenure is longer than observed (censored). The average is biased low. Kaplan-Meier uses censored customers up to the last time they were seen.

cards.q: Why is the right end of a Kaplan-Meier curve unreliable?
cards.a: Few customers remain at risk there, so one event makes a big step and the estimate is very uncertain. Show the confidence band and the number at risk under the curve.

cards.q: Why can't you compare users who used a feature with those who did not and call the gap its effect?
cards.a: Users who chose the feature differ in motivation, size and history (confounding). Randomize assignment, which makes the groups comparable on average, or adjust using a causal story.

cards.q: Why not adjust for every available column? Name two bad kinds of control.
cards.a: A collider (caused by both treatment and outcome) or a mediator (on the path from treatment to outcome) can create bias or hide the real effect. Choose controls from a causal story, not habit.

cards.q: Why does stopping an A/B test the first day p < 0.05 inflate false positives? What do you fix before launch?
cards.a: Repeated looks give repeated chances to cross the line: in a simulation of 10 looks with no real effect, about 19% of tests 'won'. Fix the metric, sample size and stop date before launch.

cards.q: Why does gradient descent zig-zag when features have very different scales? What fixes it?
cards.a: Scales like age (0 to 100) and income (0 to 1,000,000) make the loss a long thin valley, so steps bounce across it. Standardize the features first.

cards.q: Is adding an L2 penalty to the loss the same as weight decay when you use Adam?
cards.a: Not with adaptive methods: Adam rescales the L2 gradient per parameter. Decoupled weight decay (AdamW) shrinks the weights as intended, so prefer AdamW.

quiz.q: How many ways can a first and a second prize be awarded among 5 people?
quiz.why: Order matters (first and second differ), so use permutations: 5 × 4 = 20. The value 10 is the combination count, correct for an unordered committee of 2. 25 would allow one person to win both.

quiz.q: Prevalence is 2%, sensitivity 90% and the false positive rate 10%. A person tests positive. About what is P(sick)?
opts: About 16%
quiz.why: Per 10,000 people: 200 sick, 180 test positive; 9,800 healthy, 980 false positives. P = 180 / (180 + 980) ≈ 15.5%. The 90% sensitivity is P(positive | sick), the reverse conditional, which is the classic confusion.

quiz.q: Hourly event counts have mean 4 and variance 16. What does this suggest?
opts: Poisson fits, because counts are discrete
Overdispersion: Poisson is a poor fit, so consider a negative binomial
A normal fits, because the mean is 4
A binomial fits, because counts are bounded
quiz.why: Poisson requires mean = variance. Here the variance is four times the mean, so counts are clumpy and Poisson would under-estimate risk. A negative binomial adds an extra dispersion parameter.

quiz.q: You build a 95% confidence interval for a mean from n = 10 observations. Which multiplier is right?
opts: 1.96 (normal)
2.262 (t with 9 degrees of freedom)
quiz.why: With a small sample the SD is itself estimated, so use the t distribution: t(9) gives 2.262, about 15% wider than 1.96. The z value 1.96 is only right for large n. 2.576 is the 99% normal value.

quiz.q: A sample of n = 25 values has SD 20. What is the standard error of the mean?
quiz.why: SE = SD / √n = 20 / 5 = 4. The SD of 20 describes single values. Dividing by n instead of √n gives 0.8, and multiplying by 5 gives 100.

quiz.q: How do you draw one bootstrap resample from a sample of n values?
opts: Draw n values without replacement
Draw n values with replacement from the sample
Draw fewer than n values at random
Draw n values from a normal curve fitted to the sample
quiz.why: Resampling with replacement mimics drawing a new sample from the population, so repeated values appear and others drop out. Without replacement you would just reshuffle the same data and learn nothing about variability.

quiz.q: An A/B test gives p = 0.03. Which reading is correct?
opts: There is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true
If there were no real difference, results this extreme would occur about 3% of the time
There is a 97% chance the new design works
The new design improves the metric by 3%
quiz.why: A p-value is computed assuming H₀ is true, so it cannot give the probability that H₀ is true. Turning 3% into 97% for the alternative is the most common misreading. It also says nothing about effect size.

quiz.q: You run 20 independent tests at α = 0.05 and no effect is real. What is the chance of at least one false positive?
opts: About 64%
About 20%
About 95%
quiz.why: P(no false positive) = 0.95²⁰ ≈ 0.358, so P(at least one) = 1 − 0.358 ≈ 64%. The 5% is the per-test rate. Bonferroni would test each at 0.05 / 20 = 0.0025 to keep the family-wise rate near 5%.

quiz.q: A residual-versus-fitted plot fans out like a funnel: the spread grows with the fitted value. Which assumption is violated?
opts: Normality of y
Independence of the predictors
Constant variance (homoscedasticity)
Linearity of the mean
quiz.why: A funnel means the error variance changes with the fitted value, which is heteroscedasticity. It affects the standard errors and p-values. Normality is checked on residuals with a QQ plot, and linearity shows as curvature.

quiz.q: Regressing predictor X1 on the other predictors gives R² = 0.80. What is the VIF of X1?
quiz.why: VIF = 1 / (1 − R²) = 1 / 0.2 = 5, so the variance of that coefficient is inflated five-fold by collinearity. The value 1.25 is 1 / 0.8, which flips the formula.

quiz.q: Which penalty can set some coefficients exactly to zero?
opts: Lasso (L1)
Ridge (L2)
Both ridge and lasso
Neither: both only shrink toward zero
quiz.why: The L1 penalty has a corner at zero, so lasso can drive coefficients exactly to zero and thus select features. Ridge shrinks all coefficients smoothly but leaves them non-zero.

quiz.q: A logistic regression coefficient is 0.52. What is the odds ratio for a one-unit increase?
quiz.why: The coefficient is a change in log-odds, so exponentiate: e^0.52 ≈ 1.68. Odds are multiplied by 1.68 per unit. Reading 0.52 as the odds ratio, or as 1 + 0.52, skips the exponent.

quiz.q: A team uses a Beta(500, 500) prior 'to be safe' for a conversion rate. What did they do?
opts: Chose a weak, uninformative prior
Made the analysis frequentist
Nothing: any prior washes out immediately
Encoded the belief of about 1,000 earlier visitors, which can swamp a small test
quiz.why: In a Beta(a, b) prior, a + b acts as a pseudo-sample size, here 1,000 imaginary visitors. A small experiment cannot move such a prior much. Beta(1, 1) is the flat choice.

quiz.q: Which split is valid for evaluating a forecast of monthly sales?
opts: A random 80/20 split of the rows
Shuffled 5-fold cross-validation
Train on January to September, test on October to December
Train on April to December, test on January to March
quiz.why: Time series must be split by time so the model never sees the future. Random splits and shuffled folds leak neighbouring points. Training on the later months and testing on the earlier ones also uses the future.

quiz.q: In survival analysis, what is a censored observation?
opts: A subject whose event had not happened by the last time we observed them
An event that was recorded incorrectly
A subject removed because of outliers
A subject who had the event twice
quiz.why: Censoring means we know only that the event time is longer than the observation time, for example a customer still active today. Censored subjects still carry information and are used up to their last observed time.

quiz.q: A Cox model reports a hazard ratio of 0.5 for a new onboarding flow. Which statement is right?
opts: At any time, the instantaneous risk of churn is half as large, assuming proportional hazards
Customers survive twice as long
The probability of churning is exactly halved
Half of the customers never churn
quiz.why: A hazard ratio compares instantaneous risk, not time-to-event or probabilities. HR 0.5 does not mean twice the survival time. It also relies on the proportional-hazards assumption, which fails if the effect fades.

quiz.q: A treated group goes from 100 to 130 and a control group from 100 to 110. What is the difference-in-differences estimate?
quiz.why: DiD = (130 − 100) − (110 − 100) = 30 − 10 = 20. The treated group's own change (30) includes the trend that the control group also had. Subtracting the control change removes it.

quiz.q: For a convex function, a point where the gradient is zero is which of these?
opts: Possibly only a local minimum
A saddle point
A maximum
A global minimum
quiz.why: Convexity means every local minimum is a global one, so a zero gradient is the global minimum. That is why convex problems are easy. Non-convex problems such as neural networks have saddles and many local minima.
